column3: West Jordan resident, said she was speaking on behalf of a group who recently had a neighborhood meeting. Ms. Redd said
column4: Aurelia Redd, West Jordan resident, said she was speaking on behalf of a group who recently had a neighborhood meeting. Ms. Redd said there was extreme concern and deep frustration in her neighborhood related to the Community Cat Program, with cats destroying yards, gardens, and the community. She said the number of cats in the neighborhood had reached unhealthy levels and was causing thousands of dollars in property damage. Ms. Redd said the Community Cat Program had done the opposite of reducing the number of feral cats. She said she had a severe cat allergy and had needed to be administered emergency medication because of the situation. Ms. Redd said her cameras had caught 18 different cats in one night, in flower beds, sheds and garages, and on cars, boats, and trailers. She provided a packet that included a list of 17 different diseases found in the flower beds from cats. Ms. Redd said the Health Department said the neighborhood had an unhealthy number of cats, causing unhealthy conditions in yards and gardens. She pointed out there was no liability written into the Community Cat Program and implored the City Council to make changes. She suggested the City: define the number of cats per neighborhood and per caretaker; allow homeowners to capture more than one cat per day on their property, and for Animal Control to relocate the cats somewhere else; provide cat deterrents in the neighborhood; provide a service to clean up the cat feces and neutralize the cat urine in flower beds in the neighborhood to save plants and children; determine liability for property damages and provide a process to submit claims for reimbursement; update requirements for caretakers to provide food and water indoors; and create a permitting process. She asked the Council to please act now.

Alexandra Eframo noted her donation for K9 vests and expressed disappointment that K9 Maya had not been vested before leaving home. She was broken hearted over the unfortunate incident. He spoke of the responsibility Council had to ensure the quality of life, safety, security, and convenience for those who already lived in the area. Responding to a question from Council Member Jacob, Mr. Harman said his opposition would be reduced somewhat if he perceived sufficient infrastructure was in place. Anne Forester, West Jordan resident, lives near the planned Bowman’s Arrow development. She had considered living in Herriman before moving to West Jordan but was concerned about high-density development occurring. Ms. Forester asked the Council to not “Herriman-ize” West Jordan. column4: Richard Packer, West Jordan resident, said when he retired from the Army in 2018, his wife began work as a resource teacher at West Jordan Elementary. He said he and others were emotionally attached to the space. He said he was not in attendance advocated for a specific outcome but wanted to share that his friends and neighbors had been deeply affected. Mr. Packer said he and his wife had been self-appointed caretakers for the property to maintain the open space. He noted that with his current career he often found himself being the voice of empathy for citizens who were not there to advocate for themselves. Mr. Packer believed residents had not felt heard or listened to.

column4: Heather Gibson, Cedar Fort resident, said she was in attendance to support Michelle Anderson. She was a dog and cat breeder, and ran Big Hearted Breeders, training breeders all over the world. Ms. Gibson said finding a space for breeders to operate was becoming a world-wide problem. She spoke of hope and healing brought by animals, and gave two reasons the City should allow conditional use licenses to breeders: (1) in Utah, six out of ten homes had pets, and those adopting needed places other than shelters to find pets; and (2) breeders made great home-based business partners. She said breeders attracted individuals even from out of state who were looking for quality breeders and animals. She encouraged the Council to make conditional use licenses available for breeders.

column4: Chris McConnehey, West Jordan resident, asked the Council to consider reducing the lot line adjustment fee, which was significantly higher than the fee charged by other cities. He suggested the current fee was not commensurate with the staff effort required.

column4: Stephen Garlitz, West Jordan resident, said he lived in the same neighborhood as Ms. Laird. He said he purchased his home because of the lot sizes and because the elementary school was there. Mr. Garletts said he had not anticipated the elementary property being traded to Ivory, and expressed concern with the proposal put forward by Ivory. Mr. Garletts said he started an online petition that had gained more than 150 signatures in 24 hours. He encouraged members of the Council to attend the scheduled townhall meeting, and expressed concern with extra traffic on Harvest Lane. He said he hoped the lots would remain zoned for 10,000 square feet.

column3: Taylorsville resident, said she owned a duplex in West Jordan that she and her husband had rented out for several years.
column4: Jana Nixon, Taylorsville resident, said she owned a duplex in West Jordan that she and her husband had rented out for several years. She said their cost from the City had always been $86, but the recent increase adopted had increased their cost to $978. She said they had always tried to keep their rent low for tenants, so she took the Good Landlord program class to lower the fees, which reduced to $487 this year and $263 in subsequent years. She said the Utah Fair Housing laws did not apply to her because she only owned one duplex. Ms. Nickson said she felt the increased fee was exorbitant, and asked where the money was going with the paperwork all online.

column4: Amy Motta, Salt Lake City resident, volunteer with Bailing out Benji said she had spoken to the Council in the last few years about inhumane conditions in puppy mills and would be shifting her comments to consumer protection issues around puppy mills. She explained the three main consumer protection issues were: expensive vet care and training for the puppies; predatory lending; and the spread of diseases to humans as documented by the CDC. Ms. Motta encouraged the Council to review a proposed ordinance she emailed to them.
